source_title: Canada, U.A.E. sign defence, energy agreements during crown prince's visit Catherine Morrison News - Politics | 9 hours ago
source_excerpt:
United Arab Emirates has pledged to invest about $70B in Canada
Canada signs major trade, defence agreements with U.A.E.
Canada and the United Arab Emirates signed a handful of trade and infrastructure agreements during the crown prince of Abu Dhabi's visit to Ottawa.
Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan to Parliament Hill on Tuesday. The crown prince's motorcade included four RCMP horses.
Ministers from both countries signed agreements pledging to advance free trade, invest in clean power and energy infrastructure and collaborate on diplomatic training.
During a meeting with the crown prince, Carney said the visit would reinforce the countries' partnership, which has grown substantially over the past year.
Canada and the U.A.E. concluded negotiations on a free trade agreement earlier this year in what both countries called a "record" time of 47 days.
Canada, U.A.E. to expand trade and investment ties in new deal
During a state dinner for the crown prince hosted by Carney in downtown Ottawa on Monday, the prime minister said said the two countries are united in their determination to "build for the future."
Carney visited the United Arab Emirates last year. At the conclusion of his visit in November, Carney said Ottawa was working on a $1-billion project to expand critical minerals processing capacity in Canada.
At the same time, the U.A.E. pledged to invest around $70 billion in Canada.
Carney watches as an RCMP equestrian unit accompanies the U.A.E. crown prince's motorcade. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said on Tuesday that sum could include new investments in mining, logistics, energy and digital technology.
"They are actively looking at deploying that as soon as possible," he said. "They'll have more to say publicly soon."
Asked about human rights concerns linked to the U.A.E., Sidhu said "human rights never takes a back seat with Canada."
"It's important that we continue to engage, being at those tables to make sure that we raise whatever we need to raise in terms of human rights," he said.
Catherine Morrison is a reporter for The Canadian Press.
